scenes.title: AI code review for GitHub Enterprise Server
scenes.sub: GHES in the data centre, AI on Azure. A real lab, built end to end and recorded step by step.
scenes.narration: Hi, and welcome. In the next few minutes we'll add AI code review to GitHub Enterprise Server, the self-hosted edition of GitHub. Everything you'll see is a real lab that we deployed, configured, and recorded step by step.

scenes.title: Copilot code review is a cloud feature
scenes.sub: On GitHub Enterprise Server you build the review loop yourself, with the pieces you already trust.
steps: A developer opens a pull request on GHES, in your own network.
GitHub Actions starts a review job on a private runner.
The runner calls a model in Microsoft Foundry through your AI gateway.
Findings land as inline comments and a required status check.
scenes.narration: Copilot code review runs on GitHub's cloud, so a GHES instance doesn't get it out of the box. The good news is that you can build the same loop with the pieces you already trust: a workflow on a private runner, a model in Microsoft Foundry, and a status check that gates the merge.

scenes.title: Hybrid architecture, private end to end
bullets: GHES stays in the data centre (simulated in Indonesia Central)
Site-to-site VPN to the Azure landing zone in Southeast Asia
Runners on private AKS, MCP servers on a private VM
API Management in front of Foundry in East US
scenes.caption: Every hop is private: VPN, private endpoints, internal API Management and private DNS.
scenes.narration: Here's the architecture. GHES stays in the data centre, which we simulate in Indonesia Central. A site-to-site VPN joins it to an Azure landing zone in Southeast Asia, with runners on a private AKS cluster and two MCP servers on a private VM. The runners never call the model directly. They go through API Management, which forwards to Microsoft Foundry in East US over Private Link.

scenes.title: One Bicep deployment, three regions
bullets: Run from Azure Cloud Shell, nothing installed locally
Pre-flight checks quota, VM sizes and the GHES image
Validated first, then deployed with --no-wait
scenes.caption: The subscription deployment in the Azure portal while the VPN gateways and API Management finish.
scenes.narration: Step one is a single Bicep deployment, run from Azure Cloud Shell. A pre-flight script checks quotas, VM sizes and the GHES image first. Then the template is validated and deployed, and you can follow every module in the Azure portal.

scenes.title: A 45-day GHES trial
bullets: Request it at enterprise.github.com/trial
Choose Deploy on Microsoft Azure
The license file is uploaded through the Management Console API
scenes.caption: Trial confirmed: the license file is available straight away.
scenes.narration: For GHES itself, we requested a forty-five day trial license. The confirmation page offers the license file right away, and our script uploads it to the appliance through the Management Console API, together with the admin password and the basic settings.

scenes.title: No management ports on the internet
bullets: The tenant removed our IP allow-list rule within minutes
So the appliance is managed from a private admin workstation
Cloud Shell drives it with Azure Run Command: no inbound ports
scenes.caption: The admin workstation is ready and received the lab settings, the SSH key and the certificates.
scenes.narration: Here's something we didn't plan for, and it turned into the best lesson of the lab. Our tenant automatically removed the rule that exposed the GHES management ports, even though it was limited to two IP addresses. That's exactly what production should look like. So we administer the appliance from a private workstation inside the data centre network, and Cloud Shell drives it with Azure Run Command. No inbound port is open anywhere.

scenes.title: Enterprise PKI and GitHub Actions
bullets: Private DNS resolves GHES to 10.30.1.10
Certificate issued by the Contoso CA, trusted by runners and MCP
Actions storage on Azure Blob through a private endpoint
scenes.caption: From the workstation: GHES resolves privately and its API answers.
scenes.narration: From the workstation, GHES resolves to its private address. We install a certificate issued by the Contoso certificate authority, the same way an enterprise would use its own PKI, and we turn on GitHub Actions with blob storage behind a private endpoint.

scenes.title: The demo pull request
bullets: Adds discount codes to the Contoso orders API
Contains planted issues reviewers see every day
The AI review job starts automatically
scenes.caption: The pull request on GHES with the AI review summary.
scenes.narration: Now the demo. A developer opens a pull request that adds discount codes to the Contoso orders service. It contains the kinds of mistakes reviewers see every day. The AI review workflow starts on its own, on a private runner.

scenes.title: Inline findings that cite your standards
bullets: Comments only on changed lines
Each finding cites a Contoso rule ID from the standards MCP server
Prompt injection in the diff is treated as data
scenes.caption: Inline review comments on the changed lines.
scenes.narration: The findings land as inline comments on the exact lines that changed. Each one cites a Contoso rule, which the model looked up through the standards MCP server, so the feedback matches your own engineering guidelines rather than generic advice.

scenes.title: A required check, and a human decision
bullets: ai-review/foundry is a required status check on main
One human approval is still required
The AI informs; people decide
scenes.caption: The status check and branch protection on main.
scenes.narration: The result is also a required status check on the main branch, next to one human approval. The AI informs the decision, and people still make it.

scenes.title: Why this design holds up
scenes.sub: Security, reliability, cost and operations, checked in a real tenant.
steps: No secrets: workload identity, OIDC, Entra ID tokens. No public management ports.
Private DNS, VPN, retries and a strict JSON schema validated against the diff.
A balanced model tier and a per-repository token budget in API Management.
Everything is scripted, repeatable, and observable through token metrics.
scenes.narration: Why does this design hold up? There are no secrets in the pipeline: runners use workload identity and Entra ID tokens. The model output must match a strict schema and is checked against the diff. API Management enforces a token budget per repository. And every step is scripted, so you can rebuild it on demand.

scenes.title: Try it in your own subscription
scenes.sub: The workshop guide has every command, every output and every screenshot from this run. Remember to delete the resource groups when you're done.
scenes.narration: That's it. The workshop guide has every command, every output and every screenshot from this run, so you can repeat it in your own subscription. And when you're done, run the cleanup script, because the gateways and the cluster are billed by the hour. Thanks for watching.
